articles.title: Hart trusts Man City chair Al Mubarak over ruling
articles.summary: Former Manchester City goalkeeper Joe Hart believes club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak's claims they are innocent of breaking the Premier League's financial r...
articles.body:
Former Manchester City goalkeeper Joe Hart believes club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak's claims they are innocent of breaking financial rules.

City have been found guilty of the majority of 115 breaches of financial rules they had been accused of by the Premier League, although they are set to appeal against the ruling.

Al Mubarak said he is still committed to "proving the club's innocence" and the "process still has a long way to run".

Hart, who made 348 appearances for City in all competitions between 2006 and 2016, told BBC Radio 5 Live's Monday Night Club Al Mubarak was someone who has "led the club brilliantly" and is a person to "trust".

"I've heard everyone else go down every single rabbit hole, every single wormhole, every single discussion," Hart said.

"My honest opinion is I've got no reason not to trust Khaldoon. What he said is enough for me.

"I loved how he spoke. I loved the letter because that was from someone who cared about the club."

Hart twice won the Premier League (2011-12 and 2013-14) and League Cup (2013-14 and 2015-16) as well as the FA Cup (2010-11) during his time at City.

The 39-year-old said because there was "nothing concrete", it was matter of allowing things to "play out" and none of his achievements are in any way tarnished.

Hart added: "If Man City are found guilty, which I don't think they are because of what Khaldoon said, then there's conversations to be had.

"But right now I'm very confident and very, very calm. I'm very proud of what I've achieved and what I did with Manchester City and what we achieved as a team. And that doesn't change. That doesn't change until you tell me."

City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centering around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.

Hart said it hadn't "crossed my mind" to talk about the news with his former City team-mates because he "can't get involved in the ifs, buts and maybes".

"I did what I did. I lined up 11 v 11 and had it out on the pitch. I won some games, lost some games, drew some games, and I shook hands and I walked off," he said.

"I know what I did, I know what we did, and I know how it happened. It didn't feel like we were scheming or plotting."

articles.title: Can Wisconsin handle success? Fickell pushes team to continue grind after upset win
articles.summary: The Badgers beat a ranked team on the road last week. Now they have to reset and prepare for a Homecoming matchup with Michigan State.
articles.body:
MADISON – In the span of one week, Wisconsin 's situation has flipped.

The Badgers football team, fresh off a comeback win at Penn State , is a 10½-point favorite to beat Michigan State when they play Oct. 3 at Camp Randall Stadium (11:30 a.m. kickoff; Big Ten Network). Last week UW was a 10-point underdog against the Nittany Lions .

While point spreads aren't a true gauge of a team's talent, they are a sign of public sentiment, and the Badgers ' stock is on the rise after a big victory.

The key for the team will be to go about its business as if its a bear market.

"We're a team that has still continued to climb," Badgers coach Luke Fickell said Sept. 28 during his weekly press conference at Camp Randall Stadium. "Nothing has changed in the way we go about our business and so that's where for the first time, we've got to be able to handle some success and some positives and keep us going in the right direction."

The 24-20 win over Penn State gave the Badgers their first victory in Happy Valley since 2003 and snapped a six-game losing streak dating back to 2012 against the Nittany Lions overall.

The victory was also UW's highest-ranked win on the road since a 38-17 triumph at No. 9 Minnesota on Nov. 30, 2019.

That said, the film review probably brought the Badgers down to Earth, particularly the offense. In addition to Colton Joseph 's three interceptions, the Badgers committed five false-start penalties and were flagged a season-high nine times overall. Their third-down conversion rate of 26.7% (4 for 15) was also a season low.

"We know we've got to be able to play better," Fickell said. "And a lot of people will ask questions and point at the quarterback play. We know we have to play better, got to make better decisions at the quarterback position.

"But I think that there's a lot of other things that go into that. We've got to do a better job as a whole on helping our quarterback out. And so it's not just falling on the shoulders of the quarterback."

Wisconsin football schedule 2026, see Badgers' opponents, game dates

Fickell's respect for Michigan State Pat Fitzgerald runs deep

The Spartans come to town after suffering a 31-13 loss to Nebraska on Sept. 26 that also cost the team its top running back. First-year coach Pat Fitzgerald announced Sept. 28 that running back Cam Edwards will miss the remainder of the season due to what appeared to be a knee injury.

Edwards was one of the 62 newcomers Fitzgerald added to the program after he was hired in December.

Fitzgerald and Fickell played college ball at essentially the same time and have coached in the Big Ten for years as either a head coach or assistant.

That said, Fickell has respected Fitzgerald from afar due to his work at Northwestern and as president of the American Football Coaches Association.

"It's unique to see him not in the colors that he had worn for so many years," Fickell said. "But I know that he's building something, and I have the utmost respect for him."

Fickell praises impact of fans at Camp Randall Stadium

The matchup will be Wisconsin 's conference home opener and a chance to see what impact the Penn State victory has on fan attendance.

The announced attendance of 65,274 for the season opener was the lowest for the program since 1992. The attendance for Game 2 against Eastern Illinois was only slightly better (66,545).

This week UW will have a chance to ride the wave of that victory plus Homecoming weekend and what is expected to be good weather.

Fickell cited the environment of UW's last two home games – wins over Washington and Illinois last season – as examples of the positive impact the fans at Camp Randall can have on his team.

"Sometimes you think it's just if you can create a raucous environment like we were in last week, it makes it really difficult on the opposing team," Fickell said. "Well, you don't understand how much energy it gives to your team as well and so I think there's a balance there that we want to continue to create.

"We know we have a part in having success and playing better and putting the product out there that makes everybody excited to create those environments … Hopefully we can build upon the things that we've done and we'll have one of those this weekend."

images.caption: Wisconsin vs. Notre Dame Date: Sunday, Sept. 6 Time: 6:30 p.m. Location: Lambeau Field; Green Bay, Wisconsin The Badgers open the season with a marquee matchup in a historic NFL venue against a team with unfinished business. Marcus Freeman’s Notre Dame Fighting Irish finished 10-2 in 2025 and ended the year on a 10-game winning streak but withdrew from bowl consideration after landing on the outside of the College Football Playoff bracket. This game is part between the Badgers and Fighting Irish is part of the Shamrock Series that was originally supposed to be played in 2020 at Lambeau Field. But that game was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. The two teams met a year later at Soldier Field. This is the first college game at Lambeau Field since Wisconsin played LSU in 2016. (Michael Caterina, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wisconsin vs. Western Illiniois Date: Saturday, Sept. 12 Time: 6:15 p.m. Location: Camp Randall Stadium; Madison, Wisconsin Western Illinois is part of the Football Championship Subdivision. The Leathernecks have finished 4-8 in each of the last two years. Before that, they were 0-11 in consecutive seasons in 2022 and 2023. The team's last winning season came in 2017. Western Illinois, coached by Joe Davis, will play the Big Ten for a second straight season. The Leathernecks lost to Illinois, 52-3, and Northwestern, 42-7, to open the 2025 season. (Ron Johnson, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wisconsin vs. Eastern Michigan Date: Saturday, Sept. 19 Time: 11:30 a.m. Location: Camp Randall Stadium; Madison, Wisconsin Wisconsin wraps up its non conference schedule against Eastern Michigan, which finished 4-8 overall and 1-5 away from home in 2025. The Eagles are part of the Mid-American Conference and coached by Chris Creighton, who is in his 13th year leading the program. (Jordan Prather, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wisconsin vs. Penn State Date: Saturday, Sept. 26 Time: TBD Location: Beaver Stadium; University Park, Pennsylvania Wisconsin opens Big Ten play against the new-look Penn State program now led by Matt Campbell. He’s replacing James Franklin, who was fired during a disappointing 2025 that saw the Nittany Lions finish 7-6 overall and 3-6 in conference play. Campbell, 46, comes to Penn State after 10 years at Iowa State. He won Big 12 Coach of the Year three times. The Nittany Lions’ starting quarterback, Rocco Bech, transferred from Iowa State as well. (Matthew O'Haren, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wisconsin vs. Michigan State Date: Saturday, Oct. 3 Time: TBD Location: Camp Randall Stadium; Madison, Wisconsin Pat Fitzgerald has rejoined the Big Ten to take over a struggling Michigan State program. The Spartans’ last winning season came five years ago. MSU finished 4-8 overall, 1-8 in the Big Ten and winless on the road in 2025. Fitzgerald spent 17 years at Northwestern from 2006-22, has the 14th most wins all time for a Big Ten coach and earned Coach of the Year in 2018. (Kamil Krzaczynski, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wisconsin vs. UCLA Date: Saturday, Oct. 17 Time: TBD Location: Rose Bowl; Los Angeles, California After a bye, the Badgers play a third straight opponent that has a head coach in 2026. Bob Chesney comes to UCLA after two years at James Madison. Last season, Chesney was the Sun Belt Coach of the Year and led JMU to the College Football Playoff. UCLA has finished 3-6 in conference play in each of its first two years in the Big Ten. (Kirby Lee, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wisconsin vs. USC Date: Saturday, Oct. 24 Time: TBD Location: Camp Randall Stadium; Madison, Wisconsin Lincoln Riley and the USC Trojans are now in Year 3 as members of the Big Ten and look to take the next step in competing for a championship. USC enters the season ranked 14th in the country after finishing 9-4 overall and 7-2 in the Big Ten in 2025. Wisconsin last played USC in 2024, the Trojans’ first year in the Big Ten. The Trojans scored 28 unanswered second-half points to roll to a 38-21 win over the Badgers. (Jayne Kamin-Oncea, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wisconsin vs. Iowa Date: Saturday, Oct. 31 Time: TBD Location: Kinnick Stadium; Iowa City, Iowa Wisconsin looks to snap a four-game losing streak in the series against Kirk Ferentz and Iowa in 2026. The last two matchups have not been competitive, losing 42-10 in 2024 and 37-0 last season. Ferentz, 71, is entering his 28th year as Iowa’s head coach. The Hawkeyes have been the model of consistency, posting 13 straight winning seasons. The Hawkeyes are coming off a 9-4, 6-3 season with a victory over Vanderbilt in the ReliaQuest Bowl. (Ross Harried, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wisconsin vs. Rutgers Date: Saturday, Nov. 7 Time: TBD Location: Camp Randall Stadium; Madison, Wisconsin Wisconsin looks to remain perfect against Rutgers (6-0) in the all-time series with the Scarlet Knights. All of the wins have been by double figures. Like the Badgers in 2025, Greg Schiano's team finished 2-7 in Big Ten play. (Ron Johnson-Imagn Images)

articles.title: WVU vs Oklahoma St. Position Grades
articles.summary: Mountaineer fans, it’s time for the report card. We opened Big 12 play Saturday night against Oklahoma State with a lot of momentum. The Mountaineers entered...
articles.body:
Mountaineer fans, it's time for the report card.

We opened Big 12 play Saturday night against Oklahoma State with a lot of momentum. The Mountaineers entered the game 3-0, playing at home, with an offense that had been one of the most productive rushing attacks in the conference. For a while, it looked like we were going to make it four straight.

Then the tipped pass turned interception happened. I think everybody feels the same way I do, when I say that changed the momentum. We were about to go up 21 to 6, instead they went down and scored and made it 13 to 14. Even though we went down and scored and made the game 21 to 13, they still had momentum because they were able to score a touchdown on their previous possession, that was all they needed.

Oklahoma State defeated West Virginia 41-24, turning a 14-13 halftime deficit into a 17-point victory. The Cowboys scored 28 second-half points and finished with 609 total yards.

So let's grade every position group. Not just based on the final score. Let's talk football.

Michael Hawkins Jr. gave us two very different performances Saturday night. With his legs, he was electric. Through the air, this was easily his most difficult game of the season. He finished with 132 passing yards, completing 10 of 22 attempts with an interception. He was also sacked four times. You cannot finish with less than a 50% completion percentage and get higher than a B with me.

But he rushed for 102 yards and three touchdowns. That's the dilemma with Hawkins. You can see the playmaking ability. You can see why we can be dangerous with him at quarterback.

Big 12 defenses are eventually going to force him to win football games with his arm. Oklahoma State did a good job disrupting his rhythm, and West Virginia became increasingly dependent on the running game.

According to PFF's postgame grades, Hawkins received a 72.2 overall grade, which was actually one of the better offensive grades for WVU.

This position group doesn't need much explanation.

29 carries. 193 yards. 6.7 yards per carry.

That's a legitimate running-back performance. And it wasn't just Cook. We finished with 334 rushing yards as a team, with Hawkins adding another 102. We averaged roughly 6.3 yards per carry. The running game gave West Virginia a chance to win this football game.

In fact, I'm comfortable saying this, the running backs were not the reason West Virginia lost. PFF gave Cam Cook a 75.8 grade and Amari Latimer a 76.3.

This is where things get difficult. We had only 132 passing yards. DJ Epps led the Mountaineers with 39 receiving yards. That's not enough production from the receiver room.

Now, we have to be fair. The passing game wasn't simply a case of receivers failing to get open. Oklahoma State's defensive pressure and West Virginia's offensive approach both played a role.

But when the running game is producing 334 yards, somebody eventually has to make a defense pay for loading the box. That didn't happen consistently. And that's going to become a problem if opposing defenses decide they can force West Virginia to throw.

The tight ends weren't a major factor in the passing game. We needed another reliable way to attack the middle of the field, particularly when Oklahoma State began focusing on the run.

The position group didn't provide enough production to change the complexion of the game. This wasn't necessarily a catastrophic performance. It was simply too quiet.

This is probably the most complicated position group to grade. On one hand, West Virginia rushed for 334 yards. That's phenomenal. On the other hand, Michael Hawkins was sacked four times.

Oklahoma State also generated significant pressure.

PFF's individual grades tell an interesting story. Right tackle Carsten Casady received a 64.8 overall grade but was credited with seven pressures allowed. True freshman Kevin Brown received a 59.1 grade and allowed four pressures, including two sacks.

So I'm not going to give the offensive line an A simply because the rushing numbers were excellent. The run blocking was good. The pass protection wasn't good enough.

The defensive line had a difficult night. Oklahoma State ran for 220 yards and threw for 389. That means the front wasn't consistently controlling either phase. There were moments when the defensive line created disruption, but not nearly enough of it.

And perhaps most importantly, Oklahoma State quarterback Drew Mestemaker wasn't sacked. That's a major problem when you're facing a quarterback who ultimately throws for 389 yards and three touchdowns. Now, I know we're talking a lot about the passing game, but every time Oklahoma State ran the ball to their left, it was for 6+ yards at least, we couldn't even stop them in the running game.

PFF's highest defensive-line grades were Corey McIntyre Jr. at 67.7 and Zeke Durham-Campbell at 67.1.

The edge rushers didn't generate enough pressure.

That's particularly concerning because West Virginia needed to make Mestemaker uncomfortable. Instead, he was allowed to settle into the game.

Rich Rodriguez himself pointed to the lack of pressure afterward, saying West Virginia didn't get enough pressure on Mestemaker and that the quarterback was able to get comfortable. Against a quarterback who ultimately completed 20 of 27 passes for 389 yards, that is a recipe for trouble.

There were some individual positives, but collectively this group needed to be better. Isaiah Patterson posted the highest PFF grade among WVU linebackers at 70.7. But the group struggled to consistently affect the game, particularly as Oklahoma State began generating explosive plays. SECONDARY — F

This was the position group that ultimately broke the game open.

Oklahoma State threw for 389 yards. Wyatt Young caught eight passes for 192 yards. before this game, we was given up big pass place because we couldn't keep containment, and the quarterback was scrambling, causing the secondary to collapse. This game, the quarterback had a clean pocket and didn't need to scramble, and we still gave up the yardage. Our defense has a major problem.

The Cowboys repeatedly found opportunities downfield, and seven of their 12 plays of 20 yards or more came in the second half. Four of those second-half explosive plays were passes of at least 40 yards. That's unacceptable defensive production. And this wasn't simply one player having a bad night.

PFF's postgame grades show problems throughout the secondary. Nick Taylor allowed four catches on four targets for 69 yards, while Andrew Powdrell surrendered three catches on three targets for 116 yards.

Special teams wasn't the reason West Virginia lost this game. There wasn't a major special-teams collapse that explains the 41-24 final score. This group did its job reasonably well.

This one deserves some nuance. I don't think West Virginia walked into this game unprepared. The Mountaineers led 14-13 at halftime and 24-21 in the third quarter. The game plan clearly understood where WVU had an advantage: the ground game.

The problem was what happened after Oklahoma State adjusted. The Cowboys scored 28 second-half points. West Virginia couldn't find an answer. That's where the coaching grade comes down. You don't have to abandon the running game. But you have to find ways to make the defense respect the passing game. And defensively, you have to find a way to stop the explosive plays.

Here's my biggest takeaway from this game: West Virginia wasn't incapable of beating Oklahoma State. That's what makes this loss frustrating. The Mountaineers had a running game capable of controlling the game.

We had a quarterback who could make plays with his legs. We had a lead. We had the home crowd. We had opportunities. But Oklahoma State made the explosive plays that West Virginia couldn't prevent.

That's how you lose a football game even when your own offense rushes for 334 yards.

The good news? I don't think the identity of this team is broken. The running game is legitimate. Cam Cook is legitimate. Hawkins has legitimate playmaking ability, but we have to become more balanced offensively and significantly better defensively. Because the Big 12 isn't going to get easier. The Mountaineers are now 3-1 overall and 0-1 in conference play.

And that's where the conversation changes. We're not grading preseason expectations anymore. We're grading what is actually happening on the field. An after Oklahoma State, here's my report card:

QB — C+ RB — A WR — D+ TE — C- OL — C DL — C- EDGE — D LB — C- DB — F Special Teams — B Coaching — C

The Mountaineers can run the football. Now they have to prove they can stop somebody. Because 334 rushing yards should be enough to win a football game. When it isn't, you know exactly where you need to start looking.
